steps.say: Most deep bleeds stay medical, but location changes everything. A cerebellar clot behaves nothing like a putaminal one.
steps.tx: **STICH I and II** (surgery trials) found no general functional benefit from early open evacuation of **supratentorial ICH** (above tent bleeding), so routine craniotomy for deep hypertensive bleeds is not done and surgery is individualised to accessible lobar clots with deterioration.

vis.alt: Coronal brain with ruptured lenticulostriate microaneurysm, parenchymal haematoma and head CT.
vis.caption: Hypertensive parenchymal haematoma from lenticulostriate rupture. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Small tubes through the sulci changed the equation. Early minimally invasive evacuation helps selected lobar clots.
steps.tx: **MISTIE III** (keyhole trial) showed minimally invasive catheter evacuation with **alteplase** (clot busting drug) lowers mortality without improving function, keeping the technique for trial-selected lobar clots rather than routine use in every bleed, with volume reduction checked on day-seven scans and catheters removed once drainage clears.

steps.say: Speed matters for surface clots. Getting the tube in within a day improves real function, not just survival.
steps.tx: **ENRICH** (early tube trial) showed early parafascicular minimally invasive evacuation within **24 hours** (one day) improves function for lobar bleeds, making small-tube **trans-sulcal surgery** (groove route operation) the modern option for accessible clots with mass effect, with benefit concentrated in moderate clots operated before secondary injury cascades mature.

steps.say: The posterior fossa forgives nothing. Three centimetres of cerebellar blood with a squashed fourth ventricle goes to theatre now.
steps.tx: **Cerebellar haematomas** (small brain bleeds) above **3 cm** (three centimetres), with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus from **fourth ventricular** (lower chamber) obstruction, go for **suboccipital craniectomy** (back skull removal) plus external ventricular drainage without waiting for coma, with tonsillar descent below the foramen magnum as the red-line imaging sign.

steps.say: Blood inside the ventricles blocks the plumbing. Washing it out through a drain trades mortality even when function stays flat.
steps.tx: **CLEAR III** (ventricle wash trial) found **alteplase** (clot busting drug) irrigation of **intraventricular blood** (chamber bleeding) through an EVD lowers mortality but not function, so it is offered for small parenchymal clots with massive ventricular blood causing obstruction, with dosing through the drain and clamping intervals protocolised by the trial.

steps.say: A big stroke swells like a bleed. Half the middle cerebral territory gone means the bone comes off within two days.
steps.tx: **Malignant middle cerebral artery infarction** (giant stroke) with more than **50 percent** (half) territory oedema and midline shift needs **hemicraniectomy** (half skull removal) within **48 hours** (two days), which triples survival with independence in patients below **60 years** (sixty years) per DECIMAL, DESTINY and HAMLET.

vis.alt: Coronal stroke section with infarct core and penumbra plus Circle of Willis vascular territories.
vis.caption: Infarct core, penumbra and middle cerebral artery territory. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Over sixty the calculus shifts. Surgery still saves life, but most survivors need daily help, and families must hear that first.
steps.tx: Above **60 years** (sixty years) hemicraniectomy still saves life per **DESTINY II** (elderly trial) but most survivors stay dependent, so the family discussion explicitly trades survival against likely **dependency** (daily care need) before consenting anyone, with dominant-hemisphere strokes counselled for likely aphasia even after survival.

steps.say: The back of the brain follows the same mass effect logic. Squashed fluid spaces around the midbrain trigger decompression plus drainage.
steps.tx: Decompressive surgery for **posterior circulation stroke** (back brain stroke) follows the same mass-effect logic as cerebellar bleeds: effaced **quadrigeminal cisterns** (midbrain fluid spaces) or hydrocephalus trigger **suboccipital decompression** (back skull opening) plus drainage without delay, while brainstem infarcts themselves are rarely operated and managed supportively.
